Muse Spark Open is available today and brings leading agentic capabilities to your desktop for the first time on Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios.

Today, we’re releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal model with 816B total parameters (42B active) and a 1M-token context window. Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning.

We believe the future is for everyone , and that includes the freedom to run advanced models wherever, including at home. Muse Spark Open is the first model in its class to run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework.

Muse Spark Open is available today through API platforms at Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Model weights are available for download on Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models.

It runs on leading inference engines like SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp, and Unsloth with optimizations for AMD, Apple, Intel, and NVIDIA silicon. Developers can easily further customize the model using the PyTorch framework.

## Key Benchmarks

For more details about our evaluations, see the evaluation methodology report .

## Optimized for Apple Silicon

Leveraging the latest version of MLX, Muse Spark Open was optimized to run on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, and together they’re the best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop.

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

## Available Now

We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best models. The open-weight version of Muse Spark ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03-3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350.

## Safety and Preparedness

Releasing open-weight models is part of how we bring the benefits of personal superintelligence to everyone, and part of how safety work advances across the field.

Open weights also carry their own considerations , and Muse Spark Open has additional safety post-training for that reason. The results demonstrate strong safeguards across risk categories measured.

We evaluated the model in line with our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework , covering the most severe risks, and it met the thresholds our framework requires for release. Detailed results are in the Muse Spark Open model card , with a full evaluation report available soon.

## License

We’re releasing the weights under the Muse Model License with limited commercial terms, which allow many developers to use the model for free.

## Get Started

You can customize Muse Spark Open for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model. To run it on Apple silicon, use MLX, which pulls the weights directly from Hugging Face.

A frontier model that leads on personal and professional agents

Today, we’re excited to introduce the Muse Wonder series with Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, our most capable models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence. Muse Wonder brings together Active Memory and Active Focus to keep track of what matters to you and work diligently toward what you want to accomplish.

Muse Wonder is available today through the Meta Model API and Muse Code , and Muse Wonder Full is available today for Muse Code subscribers.

Muse Wonder will soon power experiences in Muse , and will roll out first to subscribers. Muse Wonder will also power artifact generation and processes that require more intelligence. And in the future, we’ll be using Muse Wonder to develop specialized models that we can bring to everyone using Muse.

## Scaling Toward Personal Superintelligence

Fourteen months ago, we began a ground-up overhaul of our artificial intelligence efforts. In that time, we’ve gone from rebuilding our stack from first principles to pushing the frontier.

When we introduced Muse Spark , we outlined our approach to predictable, rigorous scaling. Today’s release builds on that work across pretraining and reinforcement learning, delivering our most capable models yet. Trained at our gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full bring together the work of teams across Meta to deliver frontier capabilities for complex tasks at work and in everyday life — another step toward bringing personal superintelligence to the billions of people who use our products.

## Frontier Capabilities

### Model Highlights

The Muse Wonder series achieves state-of-the-art results across key benchmarks for personal and professional agents, memory, and coding.

The full results below compare Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full with other frontier models across a broad evaluation suite.

For more details about our evaluations, see our report .

The results above provide a broad view of the models’ performance. We now take a closer look at four areas central to their work on real-world tasks: domain expertise, Active Memory, Active Focus, and frontier coding.

### Domain Expertise

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full apply specialized knowledge to problems people encounter at work and in daily life, from understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information. Our evaluations include tasks in law, finance, and health that test this ability. Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), for example, requires models to work with source documents and follow detailed instructions to produce legal work products.

### Active Memory

One of the most critical steps towards useful personal and professional agents is reliable memory. Models need to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant. We call this Active Memory : carrying important context about you across conversations and actively retrieving the details relevant to the task at hand.

### Active Focus

Using that context to complete a task also requires sustained effort. Active Focus describes how Muse Wonder continues working toward a challenging goal: trying alternative approaches, working through blockers, and adapting to new information. Along the way, it asks for clarification when needed and checks in before taking important actions. We evaluate focus through FocusBench and sustained execution through SWE-Marathon, which tests work on long-running software projects.

### Frontier Coding

Coding brings these capabilities together. Building software requires tracking requirements, making changes across a codebase, and working through repeated cycles of testing and revision. Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full deliver frontier coding performance, supporting projects from small applications to complex software. We trained both models on diverse, long-running tasks to help them sustain progress across this process.

Muse Wonder builds a playable 3D kitchen game from customizable image inputs.

## Capabilities That Generalize

Two models often have similar benchmark scores, yet one seems to handle a much wider range of unfamiliar tasks. That’s what complaints of “benchmaxxing” and praise for “big model smell” both get at: a breadth of capability that popular benchmarks in a few domains can’t fully capture.

To quantify this mismatch, we investigate how performance on tasks targeted during post-training relates to performance on unfamiliar tasks as we scale test-time compute. The plot below compares Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder Full, with each point denoting performance at a distinct reasoning effort. The horizontal axis shows the model’s score on a composite representative of the tasks we focused on during post-training (“in-distribution”). The vertical axis shows the average score on a set of tasks we did not target during post-training (“out-of-distribution”).

Both of our models improve similarly on out-of-distribution tasks as we scale test-time compute. But given its in-distribution performance, Muse Wonder Full performs even better on unfamiliar tasks than the Muse Spark 1.3 trend would predict. This upward shift is because Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full build on larger, stronger base models: a stronger base yields post-training gains that carry over more effectively to unfamiliar tasks. That versatility especially matters for personal agents, which need to handle many combinations of goals, tools, and constraints — not all of which we can anticipate during training.

Working directly in a browser and across apps, Muse Wonder builds a running plan (Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors) based on personal preferences and circumstances.

Muse Wonder designs and orders custom swag based on real photos taken from a personal Instagram profile.

Muse Wonder prepares a custom wedding seating chart based on a list of complex matching requirements.

## Safety at the Frontier

Delivering personal superintelligence to everyone requires a significant investment in alignment and safety. A personal agent takes actions on a user’s behalf and might handle context such as messages, calendars, and private documents. That level of access demands a model that exercises discretion with private information and resists misuse. We trained the Muse Wonder family to lead on both dimensions, with robustness to adversarial instructions and careful handling of private information.

As models become more capable, our goal is to help people harness those capabilities safely and responsibly. Muse Wonder offers our strongest safeguards to date against CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear) and cyber misuse, while preserving access to frontier cyber capabilities for defensive use, per our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework .

Muse Wonder is our most aligned model to date, and alignment is central to how we build personal superintelligence. A full report with additional safety evaluations will be available soon.

We hope that Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full give more people the power to pursue their dreams and build the world they want. This is a major technical step toward personal superintelligence for everyone, with much more to come.

Earlier this year, our models achieved gold-medal-level performance across five high-school Olympiad competitions in mathematics, physics, and chemistry. Those results inspired us to see whether AI could also help scientists solve open research problems.

Competition problems can be incredibly difficult, but those problems already have a solution. Open research is different. There is no answer key, no guarantee that an approach will work. Making progress means trying and retrying ideas, making new mistakes and resolving them, and sometimes going back to the beginning.

Over the past several months, we've partnered with mathematicians to explore problems across several areas of mathematics. They used both Muse Spark 1.1 and 1.2 in Thinking Mode through the regular meta.ai chat interface, with no custom research scaffold.

Open research takes time. Our goal here wasn't to mass-produce papers, but to empower researchers and help them develop mathematical insights that others can understand and build on. We’re proud to partner with the scientific community to help them advance research. These collaborations were done under the following principles:

- A team of mathematicians guided the research and worked with Muse Spark to explore ideas and develop the arguments.

- A second group of mathematicians then reviewed their work.

- Each paper clearly marks which passages were primarily drafted by researchers and which were drafted by AI.

- Each paper gives credit to the earlier research and mathematical ideas it builds on.

Today, we're sharing six such papers from that collaboration. Five present answers to previously open research questions.

After completing our work, we learned that other teams outside Meta had independently announced solutions to some of the same problems using different approaches. We recognize and appreciate their contributions and clearly acknowledge their work and how it relates to ours in the papers.

## Probability: The Strict Threshold for Gaussian Ellipsoid Fitting

Aykut Arslan with Muse Spark via meta.ai . Review by Babak Modami, Alexander Roitershtein, Mark Sepanski, and Grigory Sokolov

Paper: The Strict Threshold for Gaussian Ellipsoid Fitting .

The paper answers a long-standing question about fitting random Gaussian points in high dimensions to an ellipsoid. To visualize the problem in low dimensions, imagine dots scattered on a plane and trying to draw an ellipse centered at a fixed point that passes through all of them. Our main result identifies a sharp threshold for the number of points that can be fitted in this way. Below the threshold, such an ellipsoid exists with high probability; above it, such an ellipsoid almost certainly does not exist. It gives researchers a theoretical benchmark for the limits of exact data fitting, while the behavior exactly at the threshold remains unresolved. Proof strategies were developed and revised with help from Muse Spark, under the guidance of Aykut Arslan, while four other mathematicians on our team checked and refined the arguments. We also acknowledge three independent concurrent works posted in August 2026. Misiakiewicz and Wen independently proved the Gaussian threshold. De la Cerda, Potechin, Tulsiani, and Xu established the Gaussian threshold up to a vanishing multiplicative factor. Koehler and Sohn obtained a broader universality result that includes the Gaussian threshold as a special case. These works and ours were developed independently and use different approaches.

Figure 1: A schematic showing the sharp transition from likely to unlikely exact ellipsoid fitting as the number of random points increases in high dimensions.

## Differential Equations: Finite-Time Blow-Up of Radial Negative-Energy Solutions for the Mass-Critical Biharmonic Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation

Leonard Dinh with Muse Spark via meta.ai . Review by Fazel Hadadifard and Salem Selim

Paper: Finite-Time Blow-Up of Radial Negative-Energy Solutions for the Mass-Critical Biharmonic Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation .

The paper answers a long-standing question about wave collapse in a model inspired by laser physics. To picture the problem, imagine a tug-of-war between one effect squeezing a wave inward and another spreading it out. Can the wave keep concentrating forever, or must it eventually collapse? For waves that are symmetric around a center and have negative energy, in two or more dimensions, the paper proves that collapse must happen within a finite time. This settles a question left open in 2015 and confirms a prediction from computer simulations in 2002 for this setting, giving researchers a clearer understanding of when wave collapse is unavoidable. Muse Spark helped work through calculations, test possible arguments, and revise the proof, while Dinh chose the problem and key proof ideas, and a separate pair of mathematicians reviewed and helped refine the work.

Figure 2: A schematic showing a wave becoming narrower and taller as it approaches finite-time collapse.

## Group Theory: Semiabelian Groups Need Not Be Monomial

Joseph Phillip Brennan and Milana Golich with Muse Spark via meta.ai . Review by Andres Barei and John Portin

Paper: Semiabelian Groups Need Not Be Monomial .

The paper disproves a conjecture about groups, mathematical structures used to describe symmetry. First proposed by M. Kida in 2024, it stated that every finite group with a property called "semiabelian" must also have another property called "monomial." Just as finding a black swan disproves the claim that all swans are white, one exception is enough to settle this question. The team found that exception in a group with 384 elements, showing that the two properties do not always go together. This helps mathematicians better understand how these groups are classified. Muse Spark generated the search program in GAP, a mathematical software system, that found the counterexample. Golich and her collaborators verified the result and completed the argument, with two other mathematicians reviewing the work. We also acknowledge the AI agent Nilradical , which reported a different counterexample to the same conjecture on September 16, 2026. Our result was developed independently.

Figure 3: Visual representation of the action of the counterexample of order 384 viewed as a symmetry group.

## Optimization: Tightness of the Cycle-Based Relaxation for Completed Length-Three Alpha-Cycles

Aykut Arslan with Muse Spark via meta.ai . Review by Kien Trung Le

Paper: Tightness of the Cycle-Based Relaxation for Completed Length-Three Alpha-Cycles .

The paper answers a question first posed by Del Pia and Khajavirad in 2026 about when a relaxation of a binary polynomial optimization problem captures the original exactly. To picture the structure, imagine three overlapping circles in a Venn diagram, each containing a set of yes-or-no decisions. For the family studied, the approximation is exact when each region shared by two circles (but not the third) contains exactly one decision. If any of those regions contains more than one, the approximation leaves a gap. This gives researchers a clear rule for when this particular simplification loses nothing and when it needs strengthening. Muse Spark helped reframe the problem using probabilities, identify a counterexample, and develop the proof strategy. Arslan and Trung Le checked the arguments, corrected gaps, and refined the final proof.

Figure 4: The blue approximation matches the orange exact region on the left but includes extra possibilities on the right.

## Arithmetic Physics: String Two-Point Function = Height Function on a Curve

Anindya Dey, Gabriel Herczeg, An Huang, Nicolas Jaramillo Torres, and Jacob H. Swenberg with Muse Spark via meta.ai .

Paper: String Two-Point Function = Height Function on a Curve .

Muse Spark helped researchers connect ideas from two fields (number theory and p-adic string theory), following a direction envisioned by Yuri Manin in the 1980s. Starting from a connection already known for the Tate curve, the model helped the team see how it could extend to a much broader class of curves. The paper shows that two calculations, developed in different mathematical languages, describe the same quantity. In simpler cases, the calculation comes down to counting how many initial digits the coordinates of two points share in a base-p number system. This gives researchers a concrete way to translate ideas and calculations between the two fields. Beyond helping identify the connection, Muse Spark generated candidate proofs and drafted three core technical sections, which the researchers then checked, corrected, and refined.

Figure 5: A graph model of a genus-two Mumford curve, with two central loops and trees branching outward.

## Non-Associative Algebra: On Solvable Evolution Algebras and a Conjecture by García-Martínez and Pérez-Rodríguez

Andres Barei with Muse Spark via meta.ai . Review by Nicolás Jaramillo Torres

Paper: On Solvable Evolution Algebras and a Conjecture by García-Martínez and Pérez-Rodríguez .

The paper disproves a proposed conjecture for classifying evolution algebras, mathematical structures inspired by evolutionary biology. García-Martínez and Pérez-Rodríguez suggested a test for identifying a class called "solvable" algebras . The team found a small, three-dimensional example that passes their test but does not belong to that class. The paper goes further than finding a counterexample. It establishes an alternative rule that considers whole subspaces rather than individual elements, giving mathematicians a more accurate way to understand these structures. Working from the researchers' prompts, Muse Spark generated the counterexample and proposed alternative characterizations and proofs. Barei checked, refined, and rewrote the material. We also acknowledge independent work by Hu and Wen , who reported counterexamples to the same conjecture.

## Building on this work

This work continues our investment in scientific research. We believe progress will require close collaboration between experts and AI, with results that are then carefully verified, transparent in how they were produced, and clearly communicated to the broader research community.

## Acknowledgments

We’d like to thank the researchers who brought their questions and expertise to this collaboration, and everyone who checked proofs, and helped make the papers clearer. We're also grateful to the broader mathematics community whose work these results build on.
